title: Lawson to continue in place of Hadjar at Red Bull in Madrid
excerpt:
Red Bull will continue to field Liam Lawson alongside Max Verstappen at this weekend’s Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid, with Isack Hadjar still recovering from a wrist injury.

Lawson initially stepped in for Hadjar at Zandvoort, and remained in his place at Monza, while Yuki Tsunoda returned to take over the New Zealander’s Racing Bulls seat.

On Monday, Red Bull announced that Hadjar – who injured his wrist while training over the summer break – will remain on the sidelines for F1’s first visit to the new Madring track.

“After racing for the team in Zandvoort and Monza, Liam will continue to drive alongside Max at this week’s Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid,” read a statement from Red Bull.

“The decision has been taken as Isack’s recovery continues to progress positively. While he is not yet ready to return to the cockpit, he will be in Madrid supporting the team.

“Everyone at Oracle Red Bull Racing looks forward to welcoming Isack back behind the wheel very soon.”

Tsunoda, meanwhile, remains alongside Arvid Lindblad with the sister Racing Bulls squad.

Lawson has finished the last two races with Red Bull in P7 and P14 respectively, while Tsunoda has recorded P11 and P10 results.

title: How Antonelli ‘closed the circle’ at Monza
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli made arguably the biggest statement of his short F1 career to date at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza on Sunday, superbly rising from the back of the grid to P1 for an emotional first home win in the top echelon.

But perhaps more importantly, it marked a healing, full-circle moment for the young Italian who just two years earlier made his Free Practice debut around the famous Temple of Speed – only to dramatically crash out inside the opening 10 minutes.

As Mercedes boss Toto Wolff put it post-race: “It’s how the circle closed. Two years ago, it was probably the toughest moment in his career for himself and his family. A moment where everyone doubted, including himself.

“Then, two years later, it’s the biggest glory, the biggest moment of his career that’s probably going to be one of his biggest moments overall in the future.”

Antonelli’s dramatic F1 arrival

It was Friday, August 30, 2024, when Antonelli’s F1 adventure properly began.

Aged only 18, and having starred in various F4 and Formula Regional championships, the Mercedes junior got his chance to appear at an F1 weekend for the very first time, replacing George Russell – and joining Lewis Hamilton – in FP1.

In truth, Antonelli had already been signed to replace Ferrari-bound Hamilton for the 2025 season, with his Friday run coming before a special press conference on Saturday to announce the news.

At 1331 local time, Antonelli exited the pit lane to cheers from the home crowd and set about making the day a memorable one – immediately tackling a series of soft-tyre runs and trading early fastest laps with his seven-time World Champion team mate.

Excitement and expectation built with every lap that Antonelli hustled his car through Monza’s high-speed sweeps, until just under 10 minutes into the session, when he pushed things too far at the entry to the Parabolica corner.

I remember hearing the screech and moment of impact a few hundred metres up the road in our F1 office, which had been swept away with Antonelli’s purple sector times, only to fall silent as the Mercedes slammed into the barriers at 1339.

The priority was, of course, confirming that Antonelli had not injured himself in a hefty 52G shunt, but it did not take long for questions to fill the paddock as to whether this could be too much, too soon for a driver who had already skipped F3 and gone straight to F2.

“Kimi, all good,” a reassuring Wolff commented over the radio, as he and Mercedes went into protection mode – cancelling Antonelli’s media duties for the day, and giving him time to process what had happened away from the racetrack.

When I spoke to Wolff in the TV pen a couple of hours later, he stressed: “We don’t want to slow a driver down. We’re happy to work with someone that has so much speed, that has confidence – and sometimes that can end up in the wall.

“I think he just pushed it too hard, expected from the car more than it had at that that time, and that’s okay.

“He has a lot of talent, and a lot of potential, and now it needs to be conditioned. When you invest in young drivers, these things happen, and you need to be prepared to take that risk.”

Mercedes, of course, still took that risk – Antonelli returning to the paddock on Saturday morning with a cautious smile on his face, and vowing to learn from his very public mistake in the announcement press call that went ahead as planned.

Then, after banishing the demons of his Monza FP1 outing at the Mexico City Grand Prix later in the season – “I drove much calmer today!” – Antonelli and Mercedes turned their attentions to 2025, and a new post-Hamilton era.

Looking back now, the ‘25 season opener in Australia summed up what was ahead for Antonelli. Competitive in final practice, dropping out in Q1 after a scrappy first attempt at Qualifying, and surging from P16 to P4 in the race (to finish within a couple of seconds of Russell) in tricky, changeable weather conditions.

Could Antonelli have won the Italian GP without the VSC?

Antonelli’s raw talent was never in question, but there would be plenty to work on across that debut campaign: from his general weekend approach to understanding and exploiting the car’s potential, and dealing with the huge increase in demand for his time to coping with the scrutiny of F1’s press.

Around his first Sprint pole position in Miami and his maiden podium finish in Canada, a difficult European leg of the season that featured a few more early Qualifying exits, costly mistakes and several retirements took its toll on Antonelli.

A particularly difficult Belgian Grand Prix weekend even reduced Antonelli to tears in the media pen, before a low-key Italian Grand Prix prompted a public hurry-up from Wolff, who described his performance as “underwhelming”.

In a recent interview, Antonelli shared just how much the pressure was getting to him midway through last year, and how he ultimately arrested the slide to end the season on a much stronger note with podiums in Brazil and Las Vegas.

“I think mostly last year I felt this, because obviously I’ve had a good start of the season, then I’ve had a difficult period, the European season, where I really struggled,” said Antonelli.

“In that moment I felt… I let the pressure kind of destroy me as well during that period, because I felt like I was letting down so many people who had believed in me – especially Toto, because he was the main one who took the decision [to sign me].

“I didn’t feel good in that period, I wasn’t doing well, but then I had a big meeting with the team after the European season, and it kind of allowed me to reset and just start again. I slowly found my way back, and then I had a good second half of the season.

“That gave me the confidence, being able to overcome those difficult moments, and gave me the confidence I have this year. It also made me learn a lot about myself, not only as a driver but as a person as well.”

I let the pressure kind of destroy me.Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

Putting those lessons to good use

Indeed, at the Barcelona Shakedown in January this year, Antonelli looked like a refreshed figure – appearing calm and confident both in and out of a car built to all-new regulations.

What followed, however, was beyond most people’s expectations.

After backing up Russell at the Australia season opener, where he did well to recover from an FP3 crash that might have derailed his weekend amid those 2025 struggles, Antonelli charged to four pole positions and five victories across the next five rounds.

The pressure had seemingly been lifted, the doubts erased, and Antonelli was displaying what Wolff predicted would be possible from his early days in karting.

“It kind of shows the decision we’ve taken last year, [that] giving him a year to learn while he was still 18 is going to monetise in the future,” Wolff told F1.com after Antonelli’s maiden Grand Prix pole in China. “You can see how he’s grown and how mature he is now.

“One of the things we are most impressed by is that, compared to last year, Kimi is acting with so much maturity and cold-bloodedness to issues. He’s able to compartmentalise the debriefing, talk about what’s ahead and not what’s behind with a lot of confidence, but no over-confidence.

“For a racing driver, beyond the skill of driving the car fast, that mental resilience is key, and that’s what Kimi is showing at the moment.”

Antonelli has delivered more of the same since then, only failing to finish on the podium in Barcelona and at Silverstone due to reliability issues, and building a sizeable lead over Russell at the top of the championship standings.

Then came last weekend’s Italian Grand Prix where, following an engine-related grid penalty, Antonelli took things to another level.

In what represented a huge opportunity for front-row starter Russell – who has had his own share of misfortune this season – to claw back some points, Antonelli somehow managed to extend his advantage by turning 19th on the grid into victory.

A drive for the ages, he was up to 12th after two tours, made it into the points-paying positions shortly after the restart, arrived on Russell’s tail at one-third distance, and had made an initial move for the lead on Lap 18.

Mid-race Virtual Safety Car or not, when the Mercedes drivers split their strategies, “nothing would have stopped him”, according to Wolff.

“I thought one of the two is going to win,” added the Austrian team boss. “Either George, because he was on [the front row], or Kimi, because he’s going to walk over water here in Monza, and I felt that yesterday also.”

Antonelli’s win was the first for an Italian driver at Monza since Ludovico Scarfiotti back in 1966, and puts him one step closer to becoming the first Italian to claim the F1 Drivers’ Championship since Alberto Ascari’s 1952-53 double.

From crashing Russell’s car on that whirlwind Friday a couple of years ago, to now leading the intra-team battle at Mercedes, he has certainly come a long way.

title: 7 moments you might have missed at the 2026 Italian Grand Prix
excerpt:
Monza delivered another dramatic Sunday, with the Temple of Speed bringing plenty of action throughout the 53-lap Italian Grand Prix.

On track, home race hero Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes took a spectacular victory from 19th on the grid, ahead of team mate George Russell and Max Verstappen of Red Bull, whilst Charles Leclerc’s race came to an early end on Lap 2 after the Ferrari driver crashed at the exit of the Parabolica as he fought McLaren's Oscar Piastri for position, bringing out the red flags.

However, those weren’t the only stories from the Italian weekend – here are some moments you may have missed…

In the name of Michael

Thirty years on from Michael Schumacher’s Ferrari debut, Monza provided the setting for a particularly special tribute to the seven-time World Champion courtesy of another German great.

Ahead of Sunday’s Italian Grand Prix, Sebastian Vettel – who raced for the Scuderia between 2015 and 2020 - returned to the wheel of Schumacher’s Ferrari F2002, taking the iconic car around Monza in front of the Tifosi.

The F2002 remains one of Ferrari’s most successful cars, taking 15 victories across the 2002 and 2003 seasons, but it was the unmistakable sound of its V10 engine that really turned heads around Monza.

“There is still a race to win, for my friend Michael,” Vettel wrote on social media.

Piazza Del Duomo is red – again!

Nothing says Italian Grand Prix weekend more than a Piazza Del Duomo in Milano full of Tifosi in red.

Ferrari fans once again had the chance to show all their love and support to their favourite drivers in an entertaining afternoon with Charles Leclerc, Lewis Hamilton and some special guests.

What better way to celebrate with fans than some modern music and a special DJ, with such an iconic backdrop?

South Korean DJ, Peggy Gou, was the star of the musical entertainment, and Leclerc decided to give it a shot too...but after his attempt at spinning the decks, perhaps it’s better if the two-time Italian GP race winner sticks to driving cars.

And for such a special day, a special guest was needed. And who is more special than a mother?

Hamilton chose to share this moment with his mum as Linda enjoyed a deserved response from the crowd with one of the biggest cheers of the day for her and a true Tifosi welcome to Italy.

The seven-time World Champion said of his mum being in Italy: "And my mum’s here this weekend because she’s never experienced — she’s never actually, I don’t think, been to Monza — but also particularly on a Ferrari weekend. And I wanted her to experience that and, you know, bring any of the lucky dust she can bring."

A smooth operation in Venice

The smooth operator himself, Carlos Sainz, swapped the race suit for a more elegant one to wear on the red carpet of the 83rd Venice International Film Festival.

The Williams driver seems at ease in the glamorous scene of Venice, making a statement appearance for Danny Boyle's new film Ink, wearing Giorgio Armani on the red carpet as he was accompanied by his partner Rebecca Donaldson.

Lightning McQueen turns 20

The Disney-Pixar blockbuster Cars turns 20 this year, and to celebrate this special anniversary, the seven-time Piston Cup champion Lightning McQueen landed in Monza.

While the famous movie car didn’t race in the Italian Grand Prix, the Safety Car marked the 20th anniversary with a special livery. For some of the drivers, it was a dream come true to meet their childhood hero in the paddock. Liam Lawson and Franco Colapinto couldn’t resist getting closer to Lightning McQueen.

A special helmet for a special race

It was a home race weekend for Kimi Antonelli with the Italian driver arriving in Monza as the leader in the drivers’ standings, and he could not miss the chance to wear a special helmet in front of his home crowd.

Antonelli was inspired by Italian MotoGP legend Valentino Rossi for its design, creating a new personalised version of the helmet the Doctor wore at the 2002 Mugello Grand Prix.

It featured the Italian flag, vignettes of Italian daily life (including an espresso cup and a slice of pizza), a sun, the sea, a family and then – at the back – two cartoon figures: one Antonelli, the other Rossi.

Kimi Antonelli becomes a...duck

In what proved to be aa memorable weekend for Antonelli, he also entered the Disney universe for one of the most unique moments of his career.

A cartoon version of himself, Kimi Paperelli, made its debut in a series of stories in Topolino magazine this weekend, all set in the world of Duckburg.

Speaking exclusively to F1.com, Joss Hastings, Senior Vice President of Marketing at Disney Consumer Products, explained why Antonelli was the perfect fit for the collaboration.

“Fuel the Magic is all about bringing Disney storytelling into the world of Formula 1 in unexpected and creative ways. Seeing Kimi become Kimi Paperelli is especially meaningful knowing that he grew up reading Topolino and loving Donald Duck."

When in Italy…

In a typical Italian tradition, Barilla chose to bring the Formula 1 family together for a special dinner: a moment to slow down, enjoy good food and good company before all the racing action.

For one evening, F1's Official Pasta Partner transformed the starting grid into a unique dining room, complete with an F1-inspired menu. Diners were treated to a three-course meal, with each course presented as a different 'lap'.

Few dinner reservations come with a view quite like this.

title: Mekies reflects on Red Bull's 'intense' Italian GP
excerpt:
Laurent Mekies believes Red Bull made a "step in the right direction" during last weekend's Italian Grand Prix, as Max Verstappen claimed another podium.

The Dutchman finished best of the rest in Sunday's 53-lap race behind the Mercedes machines of race winner Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, having battled with the duo and even briefly leading.

Red Bull expected to struggle against Mercedes-powered cars along Monza's straights, with Team Principal Mekies pleased that Verstappen was able to beat the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

"Today was a well-deserved podium for Max and the whole team," he said.

"It was an intense weekend, but the race showed that our pace was fairly strong. Mercedes were a bit too fast for us but we were strong enough to beat Ferrari and McLaren on merit. It was probably our best race pace in a few weeks and a step in the right direction.

"We won't be happy until we have that ultimate speed and we clearly still have some challenges to overcome, which may unlock more performance once we get to the bottom of them."

The result was Verstappen's fifth podium of the season and his third in the last four races as Red Bull continue to find improvement after a slow start under the new-for-2026 regulations.

Team mate Liam Lawson, standing in for the injured Isack Hadjar again, was unable to reach the points.

The New Zealander was due to start from the back after several power unit element changes, but started from the pit lane after further changes to his set up were made in parc ferme – while replacing a damaged front wing in the race ultimately meant he finished in P14.

"Max has been incredible on track today. He made several very spectacular overtakes and defensive manoeuvres and drove an aggressive strategy which led us to the podium," added Mekies.

"Liam showed good pace after a challenging start of the race from the back of the grid following his PU penalties. Contact with Nico [Hulkenberg] meant we had to change his front wing and ultimately killed his chance for points.

"We take the improved pace and many learnings from Monza, and look forward to the very new circuit of Madrid in a few days."

title: When F1 met Cars – Celebrating 20 years of the movie
excerpt:
A familiar voice

Although you’ll be familiar with the sound of Owen Wilson, Paul Newman and Richard Petty – voicing Lightning McQueen, Doc Hudson and The King respectively – several members of racing royalty also feature across the 2006 film.

In the first movie, two former World Champions have their own motorised counterparts. The first is Mario Andretti who competed in both F1 and the IndyCar National Championship, taking title honours in both.

He appears as himself in car form ahead of the 200-lap winner-takes-all tiebreaker race at the end of the movie, and is represented by a 1967 Ford Fairlane. The other legend who has his own presence is seven-time F1 World Champion Michael Schumacher, who appears as a 2005 Ferrari F430 at the end of the movie at Luigi’s Casa Della Tires.

Disney-Pixar also reached out to motorsport’s biggest stars for international dubbing. For Mario Andretti’s character, Fernando Alonso is used for Spanish speakers, and in the German version Mika Hakkinen replaces Andretti’s character altogether.

In the Finnish translation, two-time F1 champ Hakkinen also voices The King, with three-time World Champion Niki Lauda completing a voiceover for the same role in the German version. Giancarlo Fisichella also lends his voice to Boost for the Italian version of the film.

For Cars 2, released in 2011, more of the F1 grid got involved in lending their voices to some special characters. Alonso returned, but this time as his own animated car counterpart who attends the World Grand Prix and hangs out with Lightning McQueen in the Spanish version. Sebastian Vettel voiced race car Sebastian Schnell in the German version of the film; in other regions, the character was called Max Schnell and voiced by actors.

Lewis Hamilton also appears in Cars 2, as a character who carries the same name. He too races in the World Grand Prix, and Hamilton was apparently the only voice actor who was directly involved in the design of his persona.

Jacques Villeneuve also made a cameo as a commentator called David Hobbscap in the French-Canadian and French dubs, with Juan Pablo Montoya narrating the race car Jeff Gorvette in the Latin-American versions of the film.

Finally, in Cars 3, Hamilton, Vettel and Alonso all reprise their voices, with each playing the voice assistant of racing driver Cruz Ramirez in their respective regions.

Love for Lightning McQueen

Plenty of drivers have admitted to growing up on the Cars trilogy, with one big fan being Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson. He’s frequently taking photos next to the anthropomorphic stock car, from Disneyland to his recent trip to the Goodwood Festival of Speed.

During an interview in which he spoke about his love for the movie, Lawson was asked by F1 what his own Cars character would be like.

Lawson said in the 2024 interview. “It would have to look cool; it would have to be a cool-looking car; it couldn’t be a boring looking car. Obviously he’d have to be fast, and he’d have to race. He’d have to be like Lightning [McQueen] and he’d have to be in the Piston Cup – he’d have to win the Piston Cup! Number 30 as well.”

Discussing where his love for the movie originated, he told the media: “It was a movie that was very important to me, especially when I was young obviously. As a kid, it was a movie I watched every other day – genuinely – when I was three. Just at the age I was watching racing, and starting go-karts in the next couple of years. It was just a very big movie for me as a kid. I still watch it a lot.”

title: Vasseur promises Ferrari will bounce back in Madrid
excerpt:
It goes without saying that the Italian Grand Prix weekend is the biggest of the year for Ferrari, and over the decades the Tifosi have grown used to experiencing a rollercoaster of highs and lows.

This year’s race promised much, with Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton alongside each other on the second row.

However, they managed to trip over each other at the first chicane before Leclerc had a huge crash at Parabolica on the second lap. He escaped unhurt, but the team was left with a wrecked SF-26, and potentially some lost power unit elements.

After the red flag and restart, Hamilton could manage only P6, not the sort of outcome that anyone in the Maranello camp could be too happy about – especially Team Principal Fred Vasseur.

“Tomorrow morning back at the factory we will prepare Madrid, and we'll come to Madrid with all the energy that we need to do a good result,” he said after Sunday's race. “But it's true that Monza for us, even if I spend the week to say that it's a normal race, it's not, as you can imagine.

“And with all the Tifosi this weekend, we were expecting to give them something else as a big thanks for the support and the enthusiasm that they have. But be sure that we'll come back next week much stronger.”

The first corner clash put a renewed focus on the tricky subject of balancing the interests of Leclerc and Hamilton. The latter made it clear after the flag that he feels his World Championship bid needs more support, and that it’s time for rules of engagement to be applied.

Vasseur didn’t want to comment on the specifics of the first lap – he had not yet talked to both drivers – but he made an interesting point about prioritising a title contender.

“For sure, the outcome of Turn 1 and 2 is not good for the team,” said Vasseur. “Now to see if we have a team order or whatever, I think that the good comparison that I made was that last year Piastri was the leading McLaren at this stage of the season – and if McLaren put everything on Piastri, Max Verstappen would have been champion.

“But for sure, at one stage you have to take a decision. But I think it was too early to take a decision before Monza. Now we have time to discuss with the guys.”

While things went awry in the first couple of laps, with one car out and the other tumbling down the order, Vasseur acknowledged that it would still have been a difficult afternoon. That was evidenced by Hamilton’s struggles while battling other cars.

The team’s upgraded power unit was a useful boost, but straight-line performance was still not where it needed to be.

Hamilton reflects on 'devastating' Italian Grand Prix for Ferrari

“There are a lot of ifs,” he said when asked what a clean race would have brought. “And honestly, I can't predict. I think race pace, we showed yesterday the race pace was probably okay-ish. Main issue was top speed and overtaking.

“It means that it was quite impossible for us to attack or to defend. Or when we are attacking someone, we are draining the battery, and next straight line we are losing the position. And it was more than the pace. I think we were a little bit in a corner with the strategy, honestly. We were just stuck with the top speed.

“I think we did a step, but clearly we knew before the weekend that the fight in the race will be critical. When we were putting a bit more energy in one corner, it was even bigger the gap in the next straightline, and it was quite impossible to manage.

“But honestly, this it's not news, and coming to Monza, we knew that it will be like this. Then the circumstances of the race didn't help for sure.”

In the end it comes down to power unit performance, and despite the latest ADUO upgrade, there is still much work to do.

“I don't want to give details,” said Vasseur. “But when you have a lack of pure power, then you start to play with deployment to try to compensate in one straight line, but if you deploy more somewhere, for sure you will deploy less somewhere else, and then you are going in the wrong spiral to try to play with this when you are fighting.

“Honestly, it's not about deployment. I think deployment it was okay-ish. Even McLaren they were playing a little bit Friday and Saturday morning. At the end, we are missing pure power.”

That won’t be so critical at next weekend’s Spanish Grand Prix, where the team will have an early chance to make amends for the Monza frustration.

“It's very early to think about Madrid, and to have expectations for Madrid. I have to digest the weekend, but for sure the layout of the track is probably fitting a bit more with what we have today, and we can expect a bit more next week. But first, let me let me digest this.”

title: Max Verstappen makes bizarre Red Bull 'turtle' comparison after Monza pain
excerpt:
Max Verstappen bizarrely compared his Red Bull's straight-line speed to a "turtle" following the Italian Grand Prix after struggling against the Mercedes-powered cars.

The four-time world champion delivered a strong display to convert fifth on the grid into third, marking his fifth podium finish of the campaign.

Verstappen briefly led in Monza after overtaking George Russell early on, but was easily re-passed by the Briton and then eventual race winner Kimi Antonelli.

Nevertheless, the 28-year-old kept the Ferraris and McLarens behind and was exceptional on the brakes, overtaking several cars around the outside of corners.

It is what the Dutchman had to do due to Red Bull struggling for top speed, something that saw Verstappen overtaken with ease at times.

Asked how he was able to enjoy the race while weak in a straight line, Verstappen replied: "Yeah, I mean, to be honest, not a lot when people just drive by you like you’re a turtle.

"But, yeah, just send it back around the outside. The car is good on the brakes, so that helps, so good confidence to attack the braking zones.

"And two times in the start I managed to do that in Turn 2 and 4. So, yeah, I mean, it is enjoyable, but at the same time frustrating, you know. But I just try to maximise everything that I can."

The Italian GP was made more difficult for Verstappen due to the reappearance of his rear axle problem, something Red Bull's star driver complained about on several occasions throughout the event.

Discussing if his rear axle issue was present in the race, Verstappen explained: "Yeah, it’s still there. I mean, nothing changed. It’s just not good.

"Yeah, you struggle on the bumps, the kerbs, in the low-speed especially. It’s still like the rear axle is just not very compliant. So, for sure, it was not ideal again and costing performance, but it’s what it is."

title: Kimi Antonelli Monza masterpiece - is it the greatest comeback victory in F1 history?
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli's drive from P19 to first at the Italian Grand Prix has already been hailed as one of the finest recovery victories Formula 1 has ever seen.

The 20-year-old carved through the field with 26 overtakes and a decisive late pass on team-mate George Russell to win at home, ending a 60-year wait for an Italian winner at Monza.

But was it the best comeback victory in the sport's history? The competition is fierce, and we want to know what you think.

The contenders

John Watson, 1983 United States Grand Prix West (P22 to P1): The Northern Irishman produced one of the sport's most extraordinary results at Long Beach. Watson and team-mate Niki Lauda qualified 22nd and 23rd respectively in their underpowered DFV McLarens, yet finished 1-2 in one of the most remarkable afternoons in F1 history. It remains the lowest starting position ever converted into a win.

Rubens Barrichello, 2000 German Grand Prix (P18 to P1): With Michael Schumacher out on the opening lap, Barrichello carried Ferrari's hopes from 18th. A bold gamble to stay on slick tyres as rain fell in the closing stages proved decisive, handing him his maiden, and long-overdue, F1 victory after 123 starts.

Kimi Räikkönen, 2005 Japanese Grand Prix (P17 to P1): A wet qualifying session and an engine penalty dumped Räikkönen to 17th at Suzuka. What followed was pure racecraft, culminating in a legendary last-lap pass around the outside of Giancarlo Fisichella at Turn 1 to snatch victory from thin air.

Jenson Button, 2011 Canadian Grand Prix (last to P1): This one stands apart because Button did not start from the back. He qualified seventh, but a collision with team-mate Lewis Hamilton, a drive-through penalty for speeding under the Safety Car, and a subsequent clash with Fernando Alonso left him stranded in last place past the halfway point of the 70-lap race. What followed was a masterclass in tyre management and race reading across an extraordinary four-hour, rain-interrupted afternoon, capped by a last-lap pass on Sebastian Vettel to take the win.

Sergio Perez, 2020 Sakhir Grand Prix (last to P1): Another outlier, and another driver who fell to the back during the race rather than starting there. Perez lined up fifth for Racing Point but was spun around by Charles Leclerc at Turn 4 on lap one, pitting at the end of the opening lap and rejoining last. He then produced a methodical, patient recovery drive on a two-stop strategy, climbing back into podium contention before Mercedes' catastrophic double-stack pit error and a late puncture for George Russell handed him the lead. He held on to win by more than ten seconds, claiming his maiden F1 victory on his 190th start.

Lewis Hamilton, 2021 São Paulo Grand Prix (last to P1): Hamilton's recovery was not a single-race effort but a weekend-long fightback, from last in the sprint to fifth, then from P10 on the grand prix grid, after an engine penalty, to victory over title rival Max Verstappen. The grand prix itself was a nine-place gain rather than the deep-grid recoveries of the other entries, but the totality of the weekend is what elevates it.

Max Verstappen, 2024 São Paulo Grand Prix (P17 to P1): A chaotic, rain-soaked Interlagos delivered one of the great wet-weather drives. Verstappen sliced from 17th to the lead by lap 43 and pulled nearly 20 seconds clear by the flag, effectively sealing his fourth world championship.

Kimi Antonelli, 2026 Italian Grand Prix (P19 to P1): Starting 19th after power unit penalties, Antonelli produced an extraordinary charge through the field before pitting under a Virtual Safety Car for fresh medium tyres. He then hunted down Russell and passed him with three laps remaining to win in front of the Tifosi.

title: Lando Norris delivers brutal Mercedes verdict after Monza defeat
excerpt:
Lando Norris was left stunned after witnessing the pace of Mercedes duo Kimi Antonelli and George Russell during Sunday's Italian Grand Prix.

Norris went into the race at Monza with renewed hope of retaining his F1 title after scoring back-to-back victories either side of the summer break in Hungary and the Netherlands.

At Monza, however, despite possessing the same Mercedes engine power as their main rivals, McLaren was left wanting around the iconic 'Temple of Speed'.

Norris and team-mate Oscar Piastri finished 19 seconds behind Italy's history-making home hero Antonelli in fourth and fifth as the 20-year-old became the first Italian in 60 years to take the chequered flag at Monza.

George Russell completed Mercedes' first one-two since the opening race of the season in Australia, whilst Max Verstappen also stepped onto the podium for Red Bull.

"We've seen in past races that the Red Bull can be very fast on these types of circuits, with good top speeds and stuff, and that was again proven," said Norris, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365. "They were better than us.

"But it was clear that Mercedes are still in a league of their own compared to us. You know, we won by bigger margins over the last few races, and they were still fighting for good points at those times. We were not even close to fighting for a top two.

"Just frustrating, but we said it before the weekend. We've seen what our expectations are, and we still have work to do, which we knew.

"So it's not a surprise. We just need to work on the slow- and medium-speed corners, the stability of the car, which is just not good enough, and some straight-line speed. If we can sort that, then that's a lot of stuff sorted."

McLaren pace 'dreadful'

It was evident from qualifying that McLaren would not be in contention for a podium, and then once the race started, neither Norris nor Piastri were able to fight with the frontrunners.

Norris notably found himself battling with surprise polesitter Pierre Gasly in his Alpine once the Frenchman was dispatched by the leading trio.

"What made or broke my race was just every time I lost time to the guys ahead and didn't have a slipstream, so when I was fighting with Pierre, we lost two seconds, and I lost the gaps to the guys ahead," said Norris.

"I was slowly catching them, but as soon as we were in clean air, we were shocking. Our pace was just dreadful. We needed someone to pull us along, and then we could compete. We were more on a level playing field compared to them.

"It was almost a good thing to not be ahead for too often, because generally you would always go backwards. But then when you were behind, you always felt like you could go forward.

"It was always a tough position to be in, and sometimes you just had to be a little bit patient. For me, that worked on the final two laps, so I think P4 was the best we could achieve. P4 and P5, for us as a team, were good."

title: Kimi Antonelli 'walked over water' at Monza - Here's why Toto Wolff made biblical reference
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has extended his drivers' championship lead to 66 points following his astonishing Italian GP victory.

8 September 7:25AM

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff believes Kimi Antonelli "walked over water" in describing his young driver's astonishing Italian Grand Prix victory at Monza on Sunday.

Antonelli produced one of F1's greatest drives, starting from 19th on the grid to take the chequered flag on home soil, becoming the first Italian driver to do so since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966.

Only John Watson, in the 1983 United States Grand Prix West at Long Beach, has claimed a win from a lower grid position - 22nd.

In passing Mercedes team-mate George Russell in the closing stages, Antonelli has now opened up a 66-point cushion at the top of the drivers' standings.

Despite the engine penalty relegating Antonelli to near the back of the grid, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, Wolff said: "I thought one of the two would win, either George because he was on pole [an expectation as Russell started second behind Pierre Gasly], or Kimi because he's going to walk over water in Monza, and I felt that [on Saturday in qualifying]."

Explaining his comments, Wolff added: "It's been a while since I've seen a driver's energy levels, mindset, or behavioural pattern, and I knew that was his mission to win the race. I also chatted with his father, and the father also saw it coming.

"These are the moments when you can see how a weekend is panning out through the sessions that a special moment could come. But it's still a mechanical sport, so it can change quickly."

Wolff likens Antonelli to Hamilton

Antonelli's victory drive was aided, in part, by Charles Leclerc's crash at the end of lap two at Parabolica, although by that stage he had already climbed seven places from 19th to 12th.

A few laps later, after the restart, Antonelli had surged to fifth and was only a few seconds behind leader Russell.

A VSC much later in the race, at a time when Antonelli and Russell were dicing for the lead, saw the younger driver change tyres. A few laps from home, he made the race-winning pass as the rubber on Russell's car faded in the closing stages.

Wolff feels he saw in Antonelli's performance a similar trait to that of Lewis Hamilton during his heyday at Mercedes, with whom he won six of his seven titles.

"We had to go on a one-stop strategy [at the start]," said Wolff. "We knew he was going to go through the field.

"Then the race was red-flagged, and then suddenly you find yourself on the back foot with the medium. [But] That proved to be the right strategy.

"But the differentiator was [his] ability to go through the traffic, and we've seen it with other great ones in the past. Lewis did it at some races, and that's what he [Antonelli] has shown.

"There's just no stopping when a driver and a car are one. There is nothing that can stop them."

title: Lewis Hamilton issues clear response to worried Ferrari fans
excerpt:
Should the tifosi be concerned after what happened between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at Monza?

Lewis Hamilton has made it clear to Ferrari's passionate fans that they have no reason to worry about the seemingly rising tension between himself and team-mate Charles Leclerc.

In front of a full-house crowd at Monza on Sunday, Hamilton and Leclerc found themselves in a glaring spotlight that comes with racing at Monza, and answering questions over their relationship.

Starting from a favourable third and fourth on the grid, Leclerc and Hamilton locked horns through the opening Rettifilo chicane. Slight contact forced Hamilton onto the gravel, pitching him down the field into 10th, leading to an in-depth review as to which driver was in the wrong.

Shortly after, Leclerc's weekend ended dramatically when he suffered a 60g crash at the Parabolica. As for Hamilton, the seven-time F1 champion finished a relatively lowly sixth, primarily as the team opted against a tyre change under a VSC, even though he had complained about his fading Pirelli rubber a few laps previously.

Asked whether the tifosi should be concerned about how he and Leclerc are going racing, particularly after Hamilton complained about not being given preferential treatment at the previous Dutch GP, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, the 41-year-old said: "I don't race dirty.

"I've always raced clean and fairly, and always left space, so I don't think they should be worried about me.

"I've come into the team and tried to be respectful of space and definitely not put the team in jeopardy, and I stand by that. That's all I can talk about on my side.

"You have to speak to Fred [Vasseur, team principal] about the other side and decisions that we could have taken, but I'll keep pushing and trying to get more from the team and from our car and from the engineers in design and everything like that."

Mercedes 'mind-blowing'

Ultimately, Hamilton was left powerless against Mercedes, with four of the five cars that finished ahead of him all utilising power from the German manufacturing giant

Only Red Bull's Max Verstappen punctuated the top five as the Dutch driver finished behind a Mercedes one-two, spearheaded by Kimi Antonelli, whilst McLaren duo Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri were fourth and fifth.

Even Alpine's Pierre Gasly, who had stunned all in F1 by starting on pole position, finished only three seconds behind Hamilton at the chequered flag in seventh.

Putting aside a potential tyre stop under a VSC, sixth was the best Hamilton could do.

Describing what happened between him and Leclerc as "very bad for the team", he added: "Obviously, it put us way back in positions.

"I then tried to reset, and I was in the fight, doing good. The grip felt good, and the car generally felt decent through the corners.

"But on the straight, they were just pulling. We knew they were fast on the straight, but it was really mind-blowing just how quick they were on the straight- the Mercedes power. That thing just keeps pulling, pulling, pulling."

title: Liam Lawson criticised by F1 rival: 'It's his signature move'
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has been criticised by Audi's Nico Hulkenberg following the Italian Grand Prix, with the German deeming that "his signature move" is to squeeze drivers.

Lawson and Hulkenberg clashed following the race restart at Monza, with the Red Bull driver being forced to pit for a new front wing after sustaining damage.

The incident took place at Turn 4 and saw Hulkenberg forced off the circuit. An investigation did take place, but other than a black-and-white flag for Lawson, no further action was taken.

While the New Zealander finished the race, having to pit for repairs cost him 30 seconds, which he was unable to make up.

In the end, Lawson had to settle for 14th, while Hulkenberg went on to finish in 12th.

Both drivers were frustrated with each other, with the Audi driver stating that Lawson does not leave drivers any room.

Asked what he thought of the incidents with Lawson, Hulkenberg told select media, including RacingNews365: "Liam? Yeah, he just likes to squeeze.

"He always likes to squeeze people when you go next to him. He never really wants to leave a car's width. It's his signature. It's no hard feelings. It's just a bit tricky."

While noting that there were "no hard feelings", Hulkenberg did feel that the incident should have been judged more harshly by the stewards, based on what was discussed during the drivers' briefing.

Discussing no further action being taken, Hulkenberg added: "I need to see from the outside, but in the briefing, we said that this should be taken seriously.

"Especially at those speeds, it felt a bit sketchy at the time in the car."

title: Red Bull and Racing Bulls confirm driver line-ups for Spanish GP
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar will not return for the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid as his wrist injury persists, with Liam Lawson remaining at Red Bull and Yuki Tsunoda at Racing Bulls, respectively.

Isack Hadjar will not return to the cockpit of his Red Bull for the Spanish Grand Prix, Red Bull has confirmed.

Liam Lawson will therefore partner Max Verstappen in the RB22s at F1's first visit to the Madring.

Racing Bulls, in turn, has announced that Yuki Tsunoda will continue alongside Arvid Lindblad for a third successive grand prix.

As is well established by this stage, Hadjar fractured his wrist training during the summer break, and initially was ruled out of the Dutch Grand Prix.

The injury did not heal sufficiently for the subsequent round, last weekend's Italian Grand Prix, so the joint teams retained their altered pairings.

It was, however, widely expected that the inaugural trip to Madrid would also come too soon for the French driver, which has now been confirmed.

In a statement, Red Bull said: "After racing for the team in Zandvoort and Monza, Liam will continue to drive alongside Max at this week's Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid.

"The decision has been taken as Isack's recovery continues to progress positively. While he is not yet ready to return to the cockpit, he will be in Madrid supporting the team.

"Everyone at Red Bull Racing looks forward to welcoming Isack back behind the wheel very soon."

Driver

Isack Hadjar

French

6

How have Lawson and Tsunoda fared?

Lawson enjoyed a strong round at Zandvoort, qualifying eighth and finishing seventh as the sole remaining Red Bull after Max Verstappen's first-lap crash.

However, he endured a tougher time of things at Monza. Having taken a grid penalty to expand Hadjar's pool of power unit components, the New Zealander struggled to work his way through the field and sustained damage to his front wing whilst battling with Nico Hulkenberg, leaving him to finish outside the points in P14.

Tsunoda, on the other hand, narrowly missed out on points at the Dutch Grand Prix, finishing just ahead of Lindblad in P11.

He went one better at the Temple of Speed, securing a tenth-place finish and a point for Racing Bulls.

Although his result is under threat, as Audi has lodged its intention to appeal the stewards' decision not to punish the Japanese driver for a start infringement, which could still alter the final classification of the Italian Grand Prix.

title: Lewis Hamilton takes aim at Ferrari as Kimi Antonelli does bizarre trophy trick - International Media Reacts
excerpt:
Find out how the world's media reacted to the 2026 F1 Italian Grand Prix from Monza!

Kimi Antonelli produced one of the drives of the season to win the Italian Grand Prix from 19th on the grid, becoming the first Italian driver to triumph at Monza in 60 years.

The Mercedes driver charged through the field to lead home team-mate George Russell in a famous one-two, while Max Verstappen completed the podium for Red Bull.

There was considerably less to celebrate for Ferrari at its home race, however, as Charles Leclerc crashed out after an early clash with Lewis Hamilton had already compromised both drivers.

Hamilton eventually finished sixth, while Pierre Gasly's dream of converting a sensational maiden pole position into an even bigger result faded as the Alpine driver slipped to seventh.

Further back, Oscar Piastri endured a difficult late battle with McLaren team-mate Lando Norris, while Liam Lawson's recovery drive was undone by front-wing damage after contact with Nico Hulkenberg.

But the day belonged to Antonelli, whose remarkable victory ensured Monza witnessed a home winner for the first time since 1966.

Here is how the world's media reacted to a historic Italian Grand Prix at Monza, the 13th round of the 2026 F1 season!

🇬🇧 The Times – Lewis Hamilton blasts Ferrari hierarchy after Monza nightmare

The Times focuses on Lewis Hamilton's growing frustration with Ferrari following another painful home race for the Scuderia.

Hamilton finished sixth after an early clash with Charles Leclerc, but the article's central theme is his criticism of Ferrari's decision-making and communication, with the seven-time F1 drivers' champion increasingly questioning how the team is being run.

Leclerc's subsequent crash compounded Ferrari's misery at Monza, while Hamilton's championship hopes took another significant blow as Antonelli extended his advantage.

The Times portrays the weekend as another sign that Hamilton's relationship with Ferrari's hierarchy is being severely tested as his hopes of an eighth title continue to fade.

🇳🇱 De Telegraaf – Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies delighted with Max Verstappen podium: 'We were faster than in previous races'

De Telegraaf highlights Laurent Mekies' optimism after Max Verstappen secured third place behind the dominant Mercedes pair.

The Red Bull team principal believes the RB22 showed stronger race pace than it had in recent rounds, with Verstappen able to beat both Ferrari and McLaren on merit.

While Mekies accepted that Mercedes remained too quick for Red Bull, he saw the Monza performance as an encouraging step in the right direction.

The article therefore presents Verstappen's podium as more than simply a solid result, with Red Bull taking confidence from what Mekies considered its best race pace for several weeks.

🇮🇹 Gazzetta dello Sport – Antonelli and the crazy idea that became reality: 'If I win at Monza, I’ll eat pasta from the trophy'

Gazzetta dello Sport takes a lighter look at Antonelli's historic victory, focusing on the extraordinary promise he made before the race.

The Italian had joked that, if he somehow managed to win at Monza from the back of the grid, he would celebrate by eating spaghetti from the winner's unusual trophy.

What had initially seemed like an impossible idea became reality after Antonelli's sensational recovery drive from 19th to first, with Mercedes helping him fulfil the promise after the celebrations.

Gazzetta captures the uniquely Italian image of the new Monza hero eating tomato spaghetti from his trophy, turning an already unforgettable victory into one of the most memorable celebrations of the season.

🇫🇷 L'Équipe – Pierre Gasly, seventh in the Italian GP after starting from pole: 'Considering where we have come from, it is very encouraging'

L'Équipe focuses on Pierre Gasly's determination to take the positives from a weekend that began with a sensational maiden pole position but ended with seventh place.

Gasly admitted that starting from pole naturally made the result somewhat disappointing, but insisted Alpine had always known it would be difficult to remain ahead of the faster cars over a full race distance.

The Frenchman nevertheless highlighted his strong starts, his ability to hold the leaders for the opening phase and the fact that he finished only three seconds behind Hamilton.

For Gasly and Alpine, L'Équipe presents Monza not as an opportunity missed, but as powerful evidence that the team is finally moving in the right direction.

🇳🇿 NZ Herald – Liam Lawson completes frustrating Italian Grand Prix as front-wing damage ruins Kiwi’s charge

The NZ Herald follows Liam Lawson's difficult afternoon as a series of setbacks destroyed what had initially been an encouraging recovery drive.

After power-unit penalties and a pre-race rear-wing change forced the New Zealander to start from the pit lane, Lawson fought his way forward and had climbed as high as 11th.

However, contact with Nico Hulkenberg damaged his front wing and forced an additional stop, effectively ending his hopes of scoring points.

Lawson eventually finished 14th, leaving the NZ Herald to frame the race as a case of what might have been after his promising charge through the field was undone by circumstances.

🇦🇺 Herald Sun – 'Very nasty': Oscar Piastri roasted by team-mate as Kimi Antonelli makes history

The Herald Sun turns its attention to the late McLaren drama involving Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris, with the pair coming dangerously close to contact as they fought over position.

Piastri had briefly appeared capable of securing a much stronger result, but tyre struggles dropped him down the order before Norris eventually overtook his team-mate on the final lap.

The outlet also highlights the criticism and tension surrounding the exchange between the McLaren drivers, contrasting their fireworks with Antonelli's remarkable charge at the front.

As Piastri endured another frustrating afternoon, the Herald Sun frames the Italian Grand Prix as a historic day for Antonelli but a particularly uncomfortable one inside the McLaren camp.

title: Bernie Ecclestone arrested for second illegal firearms incident
excerpt:
Former Formula 1 supremo Bernie Ecclestone has described a run-in with Portuguese police as "wall-to-wall aggravation" after he was stopped at a private aerodrome near Lisbon carrying an unlicensed shotgun.

Ecclestone, 95, was reportedly detained at Tires Aerodrome in Cascais, close to Lisbon, after arriving by private jet from Saanen in Switzerland, where he owns a £23 million ski chalet. The former F1 chief had brought the shotgun with him for the purpose of clay-pigeon shooting.

Ecclestone confirmed he had been travelling without the correct documentation for the firearm and was held up for several hours as a result. His wife Fabiana Flosi, 49, subsequently travelled to Lisbon to try to resolve the matter.

"I had a gun that I was bringing over from Switzerland to Portugal for clay-pigeon shooting," Ecclestone told the Daily Mail. "It's as simple as that. I have guns at home there that are licensed."

Ecclestone's wife sorting out the situation

Ecclestone explained that the issue only arose after customs had initially been cleared without incident.

"We cleared customs on arriving here," he said. "I know the guys there, and they were fine with everything. No problems.

"Then a policeman afterwards asked to search the bag. It could have been [his six-year-old son] Ace's fishing tackle for all it looked like, but it wasn't."

When officers enquired about a 'blue book', the documentation required to transport the firearm legally, Ecclestone conceded he was carrying the required paperwork.

"They said they would arrest me, but after what seemed like hours, we sorted it out, but it has been wall-to-wall aggravation," he said.

"But it seems it can be put right. Fabi has gone to Lisbon to surrender the gun, or pay the tax or whatever you need to bring it in."

It is not the first time Ecclestone has found himself in such a situation. In May 2022, he was arrested at an airport in Brazil for illegally carrying a firearm while boarding a private plane, describing that episode as a "silly, tiny little incident" before being released after paying bail

title: Kimi Antonelli makes F1 history as Ferrari falter at Monza - Italian GP winners and losers
excerpt:
An extraordinary Italian Grand Prix delivered and then some, but who stood out, and who floundered?

Monza delivered everything it usually promises: chaos, strategy, heartbreak and a result that nobody quite saw coming.

A red flag, a virtual safety car and a 20-year-old Italian driving the race of his life made the 2026 Italian Grand Prix one of the most memorable in recent memory.

Here are RacingNews365's winners and losers from a dramatic weekend at the Temple of Speed.

Winner - Kimi Antonelli

Starting 19th on the grid after a power unit penalty, the championship leader turned the Italian Grand Prix into his personal coming-of-age moment.

A perfectly executed comeback drive concluded with a late move on Mercedes team-mate George Russell for the lead, becoming the first Italian in 60 years to win on home soil. Only John Watson, in the 1983 United States GP West, has won from lower on the grid - 22nd.

For a 20-year-old Italian to win at Monza, in a championship-leading car, while recovering from the back of the grid to stretch his advantage to 66 points, the title is very much his to lose.

© XPBimages

Winner - Mercedes

A one-two finish at Monza - remarkably, the team's first since the season-opening grand prix in Australia - is about as good as it gets, and Mercedes earned it.

Russell was quick all weekend and led for most of the race, while the team's apparent decision to split strategies under the VSC proved crucial in shaping the result.

The W17 was simply the fastest car around Monza's low-downforce layout. With their lead in the constructors' battle now looking increasingly comfortable, 2026 is shaping up to be a dominant year for the Silver Arrows.

© XPBimages

Winner - Pierre Gasly

Pierre Gasly delivered a maiden pole position with a stunning lap in Q3 that edged out Russell by six hundredths of a second, a result that underlined just how competitive the team's low-drag package was over a single lap.

The result even had Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff thumping his television screen; such was his frustration.

Seventh in the race, though, was always the realistic ceiling once race pace came into play, but just under three seconds behind Lewis Hamilton in a Ferrari is a result that speaks for itself. A genuinely positive weekend for a team that needed one.

© XPBimages

Loser - Charles Leclerc

Of all the places for it to go wrong for Charles Leclerc, it had to be Monza.

Leclerc lost the rear of his SF-26 exiting Parabolica on the second lap, burying the car in the barriers at an estimated 60G in a crash that brought out the red flag.

He walked away unhurt, which is the only positive to take from a nightmare afternoon at his team's home race.

Ferrari had genuine pace, and Leclerc was in the mix before it all unravelled. The championship picture has not moved in his favour.

© XPBimages

Loser - Aston Martin

Zero points from Monza is damaging at the best of times. In the context of 2026, it is another blow for Aston Martin to a season that has consistently promised more than it has delivered.

Fernando Alonso started from the pit lane after power unit changes, ran wide at Turn 7 and sustained damage that ended his race after 23 laps.

Lance Stroll made it a double retirement when a hydraulic failure brought out the VSC around half-distance. Adrian Newey's first full season with the team is not going to plan, and there is still a long way to go.

© XPBimages

Loser - Ferrari

Leclerc's early crash was damaging enough, but the deeper story of Ferrari's Italian Grand Prix was one of a team that does not yet know what it wants to be. The rules of engagement between Lewis Hamilton and Leclerc remain frustratingly unclear, and Monza did little to resolve that.

It is a dynamic that cost the team at Zandvoort, where Hamilton sat behind Leclerc on fresher tyres while Mercedes executed a clean swap between their drivers without hesitation. Ferrari hesitated then, and the uncertainty has not gone away.

Hamilton's sixth-place finish, on worn tyres after Ferrari chose not to act under the VSC, felt like a consequence of the same indecision rather than a considered strategic call.

With two strong drivers who have differing views on the car and contrasting setup preferences, the risk is that Ferrari ends up serving neither particularly well. At their home race, in front of the tifosi, that is a problem they can no longer afford to leave unresolved.

title: Max Verstappen responds to Loek Hartog's life-saving act
excerpt:
The remarkable actions of Loek Hartog over the weekend have not gone unnoticed by Max Verstappen, after Hartog saved the life of fellow racing driver Ollie Millroy.

The four-time F1 drivers' champion took a moment after the Italian Grand Prix at Monza to praise his fellow Dutchman for an act of bravery that captured the attention of the entire motorsport world.

Hartog was competing in the fourth round of the China GT Championship at the Shanghai International Circuit, driving his Porsche 911 GT3 R EVO, when a chain-reaction collision engulfed rival Millroy's Ferrari in flames.

The British driver was trapped in the cockpit as marshals stood hesitantly on the sideline, seemingly unsure how to respond to the burning wreck.

Hartog did not hesitate. He brought his own car to a halt, sprinted towards the fire, grabbed a fire extinguisher from a marshal and physically hauled Millroy to safety. The entire rescue took just 49 seconds.

Following the Italian Grand Prix, in which Verstappen finished third behind Mercedes pair Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, he was asked by Viaplay for his reaction to his compatriot's intervention. The Red Bull driver's admiration was plain to see.

"Yes, that is incredible. He did that really well. A lot of respect for that. Without him, he wouldn't have survived. Yes, very special," said Verstappen.

Millroy sustained five broken ribs, a broken collarbone, a broken hand and a bruised lung, but survived the incident.

From his hospital bed, he said that he owes his life to Hartog. The rescue has been praised globally by media outlets, fellow drivers and fans alike.
